displayQuote: Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change

meta.title: Who really said "Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Pinned on Stephen Hawking, but there's no source for it. The line is a compressed echo of a 1963 Darwin paraphrase by professor Leon Megginson.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change'?
meta.ogDescription: There's no evidence Hawking said it. The phrase descends from Leon Megginson's 1963 restatement of Darwin, not from Hawking or Darwin.

answer.label: Not Stephen Hawking — an unsourced modern paraphrase
answer.authorName: Unknown; descended from Leon C. Megginson’s 1963 Darwin paraphrase
answer.authorDates: Exact wording has no documented primary source
answer.sourceLine: There is no record of Stephen Hawking writing or saying this line — it appears in none of his books, papers, or documented interviews, and Wikiquote lists no sourced instance of it. The sentence is a compressed, anonymised echo of a much older meme: Quote Investigator traces the “survives by adapting to change” idea to management professor Leon C. Megginson, who in 1963 paraphrased Darwin. Tellingly, Megginson set intelligence against adaptability rather than equating them — so the tidy “intelligence is the ability to adapt” wording matches neither Hawking nor Megginson. It was simply pinned on Hawking’s famous name.

source.heading: Where the line actually comes from

docMeta.dd: No documented source — an unsourced modern paraphrase

source.excerpt: According to Darwin’s Origin of Species, it is not the most intellectual of the species that survives; it is not the strongest that survives; but the species that survives is the one that is able best to adapt and adjust to the changing environment in which it finds itself.
trail: Quote Investigator traces the “survives by adapting to change” line to a 1963 speech by management professor Leon C. Megginson — a paraphrase of Darwin — and does not mention Hawking at all.
Megginson’s words appeared in “Lessons from Europe for American Business” (Southwestern Social Science Quarterly, 1963); over the decades they were streamlined and re-pinned onto famous names.
Wikiquote’s Stephen Hawking page records no sourced words of his that match this line.
source.cutTag: the 1963 ancestor, not a Hawking quote
source.excerptNote: Leon C. Megginson, 1963 — the documented ancestor of the whole “adapt to change” quote family. Note that it contrasts intelligence with adaptability; the “intelligence is the ability to adapt” line credited to Hawking is a later, unsourced compression that no primary source supports.

source.rightsNote: The exact wording “Intelligence is the ability to adapt to change” has no identified author or first publication, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted. Its closest documented ancestor — Leon C. Megginson’s 1963 sentence — is a distinct line that remains in copyright, but that is not the quote credited to Hawking.

author.name: Leon C. Megginson
author.heading: About Leon C. Megginson
author.metaLine: 1921–2010 · American management professor, Louisiana State University
author.bio: Leon C. Megginson was an American professor of management and marketing who taught for decades at Louisiana State University. In a 1963 address later published as “Lessons from Europe for American Business,” he offered his own loose restatement of Darwin’s On the Origin of Species — arguing that the species that survives is the one best able to adapt to a changing environment. He never claimed to be quoting Darwin verbatim, but over the following decades his paraphrase was streamlined and re-pinned onto Darwin, and later onto other famous names.

cite.sourceCitation: Leon C. Megginson, “Lessons from Europe for American Business,” Southwestern Social Science Quarterly 44, no. 1 (1963): 3–13 — the documented ancestor of the “adapt to change” quote family. No primary source exists for the exact wording attributed to Stephen Hawking.

misattribution.heading: A textbook magnet-name misattribution
misattribution.intro: This is one of the internet’s favourite “Hawking” quotes — and there is no evidence he ever said or wrote it.

items.why: The line appears in none of Hawking’s books, lectures, or documented interviews, and Wikiquote lists no sourced instance. It spread across quote sites and social media, and The Washington Post publicly asked in 2018 whether he really said it.
The broader “it is the most adaptable that survives” idea is routinely credited to Darwin, but Quote Investigator found it nowhere in Darwin’s writings — it is Megginson’s 1963 paraphrase.

misattribution.truthLine: The nearest real source is management professor Leon C. Megginson, who in 1963 paraphrased Darwin — and even he did not equate intelligence with adaptation (Quote Investigator).

context.heading: Why it stuck to Hawking
lead: Stephen Hawking — a physicist who reshaped cosmology while living for decades with motor-neurone disease — is a natural magnet for an aphorism about adapting to change. That resonance is part of why the misattribution stuck so hard, especially in the wave of tributes after his death in March 2018.

The quote also rides on an older, equally false Darwin meme. Once a line about surviving-by-adapting was loose in the culture, compressing it to “intelligence is the ability to adapt to change” and attaching it to a beloved genius was an easy, unverified step.
context.pull: A line about adapting, pinned to a man the world watched adapt.
